findings.source_passage: He stood alone. He had no master--hardly even his father. He had no scholars--hardly even his sons.
findings.source_locator: paragraph on Boston standards, after listing Ticknor, Prescott, Longfellow, Motley, O. W. Holmes
findings.why_it_matters: This three-sentence climax is one of the most critically-cited formulations about Charles Francis Adams's isolation in the entire book; its rhetorical rhythm (the paired negations, the escalating paradox) is unmistakably signature Adams. Its omission removes the interpretive keystone of the whole portrait of the father.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full Boston-standards paragraph culminating in 'He stood alone. He had no master—hardly even his father. He had no scholars—hardly even his sons.' before or within the existing Charles Francis Adams characterization block.

findings.source_passage: named candidates for the general election in November: for President, Martin Van Buren; for Vice-President, Charles Francis Adams.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'The parallel, as concerned bias of education, was complete when'
findings.why_it_matters: The VP nomination is the exact hinge that makes the 1848/1776 parallel 'complete'—Adams calls it so explicitly. Without it, the entire education-as-political-destiny argument for this segment loses its documentary anchor, and the reader cannot understand why the stamp of 1848 is 'almost as indelible as the stamp of 1776.'
findings.suggested_fix: Insert the Free Soil Buffalo convention passage with the Van Buren/Charles Francis Adams ticket names; this is the payoff of the 1848/1776 parallel that the draft otherwise reproduces.

findings.source_passage: the fourth, being of less account, was in a way given to his mother, who named him Henry Brooks, after a favorite brother just lost.
findings.source_locator: opening paragraph, Peter Chardon Brooks genealogy
findings.why_it_matters: The entire opening genealogical paragraph is absent, including the famous self-deprecating irony of Henry being 'of less account'—one of the most quoted self-presentations in the book and a foundational voice-establishing gesture for the chapter.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the opening paragraph on Peter Chardon Brooks's estate, the seven children, and especially the 'being of less account' formulation for Henry; this is the chapter's announced subject and its first ironic signature.

findings.source_passage: his father gave him a writing-table in one of the alcoves of his Boston library, and there, winter after winter, Henry worked over his Latin Grammar and listened to these four gentlemen discussing the course of anti-slavery politics.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'As the boy grew up to be ten or twelve years old'
findings.why_it_matters: The writing-table scene is the central image of the boy's political education by absorption—it anchors the chapter's educational argument concretely and bridges the abstract discussion of Adams/Palfrey/Dana/Sumner to the boy's actual experience; its absence loses a key scene.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the alcove writing-table passage, including the Novanglus proof-reading anecdote and the sardonic observation about learning to 'be dull in some different way.'

findings.source_passage: Sumner was the boy's ideal of greatness; the highest product of nature and art. The only fault of such a model was its superiority which defied imitation... Mr. Sumner was a different order--heroic.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'The boy Henry worshipped him'
findings.why_it_matters: The draft retains 'The boy Henry worshipped him' but drops the escalating characterization ('highest product of nature and art,' 'a different order—heroic'), which is the rhetorical climax of the Sumner portrait and critically cited in studies of Adams's hero-worship.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full closing sentences of the Sumner worship passage, especially 'a different order—heroic,' which is tonally distinct and interpretively important.

findings.source_passage: the eldest child, Louisa, was one of the most sparkling creatures her brother met in a long and varied experience of bright women... while Mr. Adams, who talked relatively little, was always a good listener, and laughed over a witticism till he choked.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'The children reached manhood without knowing religion'
findings.why_it_matters: The dinner-table paragraph humanizes the entire Adams household with specific, affectionate characterizations—Louisa 'sparkling,' John 'best talkers in Boston,' Sumner 'smiled grandly,' and the father 'laughed till he choked'—voice-establishing domestic texture entirely absent from the draft.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the dinner-table paragraph with its individual characterizations, particularly the closing image of Mr. Adams laughing till he choked, which uniquely softens the formal portrait of the father.

findings.source_passage: The passionate hatred of school methods was almost a method in itself... He always reckoned his school-days, from ten to sixteen years old, as time thrown away.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'In any and all its forms, the boy detested school'
findings.why_it_matters: The paradox that 'passionate hatred of school methods was almost a method in itself' is a signature Adamsian inversion and the chapter's core educational thesis in miniature; the draft omits this and gives only a pale summary of the school-failure argument.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the passage on school-hatred as method, the 'time thrown away' verdict, and the specific statement about the four necessary tools (Mathematics, French, German, Spanish) as a coherent block; the draft has the tools list but without the framing hatred-as-method paradox.

summary: The draft has three high-severity failures—the iconic 'He stood alone' sentence, the VP nomination payoff of the 1848/1776 parallel, and the entire Brooks genealogical opening with its foundational 'of less account' irony—plus four medium-severity losses of voice and interpretive content, requiring regeneration.
